yogapaṭṭa
(‘cloth of योग’)
------------------------------------------
This is the band of cloth used for holding the crossed legs firmly in position while practising yogic meditation. It goes round the two legs at the level of the knees, the legs being slightly raised. It may be wound round in other ways also.
Yogapaṭṭa is a technical term used in the process of giving सṁन्यास or monastic vows. It is the act of giving the monastic name to the newly ordained disciple after holding a cloth over his head and reciting some verses from the Bhagavadgītā (11.15 to 33). The disciple is, hence forward, competent to ordain others into सṁन्यास and guide them.

yogi
(‘one who has attained concentration of मिन्द्’)
------------------------------------------
In general, anyone who is practising any kind of the well-known yogas (See YOGA for details.) can be called a योगि.
The Vyāsabhāṣya on the Yogasūtras (3.51) of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) describes four kinds of yogis.
See PRATHAMAKALPIKA for details.
The Haṭhayogapradīpikā (4.106-112), a standard work on हठयोग, describes in detail the condition of a yogi—considered as mukta or emancipated—especially in समाधि (superconscious state). He has transcended all dualities of mundane life.

yogāṅga
------------------------------------------
This is a technical term used in वीरशैविस्म्. See under ŚAIVISM.
The word may also indicate one of the eight steps of योग as given in the योगदर्शन of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.).

Yogānarasiṁha
------------------------------------------
This is one of the variant forms of नरसिṁह, the fourth इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु in the Daśāvatāra list.
Here, नरसिṁह is shown as sitting, absorbed in deep yogic meditation. There is a band, ‘yogapaṭṭa’ binding his legs at the level of the knees. Of the four hands, the upper two carry the चक्र (discus) and शङ्ख (conch). The two lower hands are resting on the knees.

yogajapratyakṣa
(‘direct perception born out of [the practice of] योग’)
------------------------------------------
Normally, the knowledge that we get from प्रत्यक्ष or direct perception, is derived through our five ज्ञानेन्द्रियस् or organs of knowledge like the eyes and the ears. This knowledge is very limited due to various factors such as defects of the organs or external obstacles. However, when the योगि attains the state of समाधि, the powers of his मिन्द् are heightened to such an extent that he can ‘see’ anything he likes, even if such an object is hidden in the ground or obstructed by impervious things like a wall or is at a great distance. This is called yogajapratyaka. See Yoga-sūtras (1.35 and 3.25).

yogavighnas
(‘hindrances to योग’)
------------------------------------------
Yogavighnas, obstacles and hind-rances to योग (concentration and meditation leading to God-realisation or libera-tion), are many and varied. They have been listed by some works such as the Śivasaṁhitā (5.1 onwards), Yogakuṇḍali Upaniṣād (1.56 to 61) and Yogatattva Upaniṣad (30, 31).
They are: भोग (enjoyment); धर्म (ritualism); ज्ञान (intellectual knowledge); divāsupti (sleeping during daytime); viṣamāsanadoṣa (defects of āsanas); सṁशय (doubts); pramattatā (conceit); आलस्य (laziness); निद्रा (excessive sleep); bhrānti (anomalous understanding); strīlaulya (sexuality); mṛgatṛṣṇā (illusory and vain desires).
The Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) has listed nine obstacles called अन्तरायस् and five more that create tensions in the मिन्द् (vide 1.30 and 31). See ANTARĀYAS for details.

Yoginī Tantra
------------------------------------------
This is a voluminous work of two Khaṇḍas or sections, belonging to the tantra-group. It has 2795 verses distribu-ted among 27 sargas or chapters. The first Khaṇḍa or section contains 19 sargas (and 1291 verses) whereas the second Khaṇḍa has 8 sargas plus a परिशिष्ट (appendix) (1504 verses).
A very brief account of the contents only can be given here:
First Khaṇḍa
Sarga 1 (56 Verses)
Greatness of the गुरु in spiritual life.
Sarga 2 (74 Verses)
Various types of japamālās prepared out of śankha (conch) or मणि (pearl), the number of beads as also the results of using them; some details connected with जप (repetition of the मन्त्र) such as suitable time and place; on the मोथेर् Kālī and the greatness of काशी.
Sarga 3 (66 Verses)
Details about preparing a kavaca (esoteric diagram with a मन्त्र inscribed on a suitable material), by wearing which diseases can be averted and other persons can be mesmerised.
Sarga 4 (74 Verses)
Details of षट्कर्मस् of वामाचार cults. (See ṢAṬKARMAS.)
Sarga 5 (77 Verses)
How लक्ष्मी became a बिल्व tree (Aegle marmelos), worshipped the शिव-लिङ्ग and got a place on the chest of विष्णु.
Sarga 6 (73 Verses)
Description of two types of sādhakas, the ‘divya’ and the ‘vīra’; पञ्चमकारस् (the five ‘m’s.) (See under TANTRAS.)
Sarga 7 (61 Verses)
Svapnāvatī-विद्या (repetition of a special मन्त्र 108 times per day for 4 years by which one gets a vision of the goddess); mṛtasañjīvinīvidyā (the मन्त्र by which a dead person can be revived).
Sarga 8 (72 Verses)
Manifestation of Kālī from मोथेर् पार्वती.
Sarga 9 (75 Verses)
Kālī assigns duties to ब्रह्मा, विष्णु and शिव.
Sarga10 (63 Verses)
Kālī infills विष्णु, ब्रह्मा and शिव with इच्छाशक्ति, क्रियाशक्ति and ज्ञानशक्ति respectively.
Sarga 11 (69 Verses)
‘Kālīvidyā’ described in detail with the मन्त्र, पूजा (worship), हवन or होम, ध्यान (meditation) and other details.
Sarga 12 (74 Verses)
The greatness and importance of the famous pilgrim centre कामाख्या in Assam.
Sarga 13 (61 Verses)
On कर्म and its fruits; the inevitability of कर्म.
Sarga 14 (81 Verses)
About the non-Vedic races like यवनस्, saumaras and म्लेच्छस् as also their mutual conflicts.
Sarga 15 (67 Verses)
Killing of the demon Keśi by Kālī; the greatness of the hill गोवर्धन.
Sarga 16 (59 Verses)
Destruction of Tripurāsura; लिबेरतिओन् of those who die at काशी.
Sarga 17 (53 Verses)
Destruction of the demon Kolāsura by Kālī; significance and practice of ‘Kumārīpūjā’ (worshipping Kālī through a Kumārī or young girl).
Sarga 18 (55 Verses)
Birth of the river गङ्गा and its greatness eulogised.
Sarga 19 (81 Verses)
Karāla भैरव gets transformed into Krodha भैरव.
Second Khaṇḍa
Sarga 1 (60 Verses)
Names of some शक्तिपीठस् like Kāmarūpa and Jālandhara as also the minor places associated with the देवी.
Sarga 2 (68 Verses)
Some details connected with तीर्थयात्रा or पिल्ग्रिमगे like suitable dates.
Sarga 3 (77 Verses)
Some places of पिल्ग्रिमगे and their importance.
Sarga 4 (138 Verses)
Different pilgrim centres associated with शिव and the names of his several aspects.
Sarga 5 (342 Verses)
This long section deals mainly with the ceremonial offering of piṇḍas (rice-balls) during śrāddha ceremonies.
Sarga 6 (187 Verses)
Ritual methods of taking bath, worship of deities, giving gifts etc., in places of पिल्ग्रिमगे.
Sarga 7 (242 Verses)
The method of devīpūjā or worship of the Divine मोथेर् is described in detail along with the fruits thereof.
Sarga 8 (123 Verses)
This contains detailed descriptions of various places of पिल्ग्रिमगे as also the religious rites to be conducted there.
Pariśiṣṭa (Appendix) (264 verses)
A few more places of पिल्ग्रिमगे, but less known are mentioned here.

yogamudrā
------------------------------------------
Mudrās or handposes are common to the images of gods and sages.
In the योगमुद्रा, the left palm facing upwards is kept on the lap of the sitting image, with the right one, in the same fashion, being placed over it. It indicates deep meditation.

yogakṣema
------------------------------------------
This word has been used in the Ṛgveda (10.166.5) in the sense of earning wealth (yoga) and protecting it after earning (kṣema). In the धर्मशास्त्रस् the word has been interpreted as iṣṭā or sacrifices (for योग) and पूर्त or public works of charity (for kṣema). Another meaning is comfortable living (vide गौतम Dharmasūtras 9.63).
Some others have declared that it indicates the royal ministers and the royal priest since they bring about the welfare of the nation (vide Mitākṣarā—commentary on Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.119).
However, in the well-known verse of the Bhagavadgītā (9.22), all the commentators agree that योग means getting what one wants, and kṣema, protecting it.
Attaining God is योग. मोक्ष or freedom from transmigration is kṣema. This can be a philosophical interpretation.

Yoga-Yājñavalkya
------------------------------------------
This is a small work on योग attri-buted to the great sage याज्ञवल्क्य. It has 506 verses spread over 12 chapters.
In an assembly of sages, Gārgī (considered the best among the experts in the knowledge of ब्रह्मन्) and Maiteryī (Yajñavalkya’s first wife, considered as the best among married women) were also present. Gārgī prostrated herself before याज्ञवल्क्य and requested him to teach the essence of योग. The sage agreed and expounded its eight limbs viz., यम (ten disciplines like अहिṁसा or non-violence), नियम (also ten disciplines like तपस् or austerity), आसन (bodily postures of eight kinds), प्राणायाम (control of breath with appropriate mantras), प्रत्याहार (withdrawal of senses), धारणा (fixing the मिन्द् on the object of concentration and is of five kinds), ध्यान (meditation) and समाधि (superconscious experience).
Other important points stressed in this work are: performance of actions enjoined by Vedic injunctions; posture for controlling the prāṇic energy; rousing of the कुण्डलिनी power; appearance of some psychic experiences indicating the progress in the path of योग.

Yoginīhṛdaya
------------------------------------------
This is one of the important texts of the tantra group of literature.
The तन्त्रस् are sometimes classified into two varieties: The निगम and the āgama. In the former, it is the देवी (the Divine मोथेर्) who is the teacher and शिव, the disciple. In the latter however, the roles are reversed.
In this work it is शिव who teaches the esoteric truths to the देवी.
It has 377 ślokas (verses in the anuṣṭubh metre) spread over 3 paṭalas or chapters.
There are two Sanskrit commen- taries: Setubandha by Bhāskararāya- makhin or Bhāsurānandanātha (17th century A. D.);
Dīpikā by Amṛtānandanātha.
Bhāskararāyaḥa-makhin treats this work as the last part of another well-known work (its last three chapters, 6th to 8th), the Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava, also called Vāmakeśvaratantra.
A brief summary of the work may now be given here:
First Paṭala (Cakrasaṅketanirūpaṇam—verses 86)
This esoteric wisdom can be given to an aspirant only after testing him for at least six months. It should never be imparted to disciples of other gurus, or atheists or lazy persons.
This is then followed by a detailed description of the श्रीचक्र. (See ŚRĪCAKRA.)
It is interesting to note that the nine parts of the श्रीचक्र are given different names such as Sarvānandamayacakra, Sarvarakṣākaracakra, Trailokyamohanacakra and so on, by worshipping which, specified results may be obtained.
Second Paṭala (Mantrasaṅketanirūpaṇam—verses 85)
In the beginning, nine nyāsas (puri-ficatory processes) of various limbs with appropriate विद्यास् or mantras like karaśuddhividyā for the extremities of the feet etc., are described.
The sādhaka is then advised to think of the various aspects of the देवी like Tripurā, Tripureśvarī and so on in the various चक्रस् of the body like the well- known six चक्रस् (ādhāra, स्वाधिष्ठान etc.).
Six kinds of meanings of mantras are possible. They are: bhāvārtha (meaning as revealed by the letters of the मन्त्र); sampradāyārtha (meaning according to the tradition, received from the गुरु or preceptor); nigarbhārtha (knowledge of the unity of the deity, the गुरु and oneself) kaulikārtha (knowledge of the unity of the श्रीचक्र, the Divine मोथेर्, the मन्त्र, the गुरु and one’s Self); rahasyārtha (knowledge of the identity of the कुण्डलिनी and the मन्त्र); mahātattvārtha (knowledge of the unity of the jīvātman with शिव).
The section closes with the eulogy of गुरु’s grace, by which alone all this knowledge can be got.
Third Paṭala (Pūjāsaṅketanirūpaṇa—206 verses)
This paṭala is devoted mainly to various steps connected with पूजा or ritualistic worship.
Pūjā is described as of three types: parāpūjā, aparāpūjā and parā-aparā-पूजा.
In parāpūja one has to think of the identity of the गुरु, the देवी in the heart and one’s आत्मन्. Aparāpūjā is the regular ritualistic worship of the श्रीचक्र. The parā-aparā-पूजा is a mixture of these two steps.
The text then describes various nyāsas (ritual purification of limbs) including the न्यास of श्रीचक्र.
The other topics dealt with are: removal of obstacles, worship of सूर्य and other प्लनेत्स्, worship of the sandals of गुरु, पूजा of श्रीचक्र in detail, method of जप, तर्पण (satiating with water) and concluding the whole worship.
The treatise ends with the strict instruction that this knowledge should never be imparted to unworthy persons.

Yoganidrā
(‘sleep-like condition in योग’)
------------------------------------------
After प्रलय or dissolution of the world, before next च्रेअतिओन्, God (Viṣṇu) is said to rest in sleep. It is actually a sleep-like condition and is called योगनिद्रा.
Iconographical works like the Pādma-saṁhitā describe योगनिद्रा as a goddess, dark in colour, resting on a cot in a half sleepy state. She has two hands, the left carrying a noose and the right a pānapātra or a bowl of intoxicating drink.

Yogacūdāmaṇi Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is one of the twenty minor उपनिषद्स् called योग उपनिषद्स्. It belongs to the Sāmaveda.
There are 121 ślokas occasionally interspersed with prose passages. There is one commentary by Upaniṣad Brahmendra who has written vivaraṇas or explanations on 108 उपनिषद्स्.
The work opens with listing six yogāṅgas or limbs of योग. They are: आसन (posture); prāṇasaṁrodha (prāṇāyāma or breath-control); प्रत्याहार (withdrawal of senses); धारणा (fixing the मिन्द् on the object of concentration); ध्यान (meditation) and समाधि (perfect concentration resulting in superconscious experience).
This is followed by a description of the six चक्रस् or psychic centres in the body. They are: मूलाधार (at the root of the spinal column); स्वाधिष्ठान (at the root of the sexual organ); maṇipūra (at the navel); anāhata (at the level of the heart); viśuddha (at the level of the throat); ājñā (between the eyebrows).
Then comes a brief exposition of the five major prāṇas like प्राण and अपान, and the five minor prāṇas (called upaprāṇas) like नाग, कूर्म and so on. The जीव (bound सोउल्) moves about because of their activity.
Next comes ajapāgāyatrī. It is the repetition of the मन्त्र haṁsaḥ so’haṁ coupled with breathing.
Now, a description of rousing the कुण्डलिनी and making it move up the सुषुम्ना canal is given. Incidentally, the regimen of ड़ोओद् for a योगि is also mentioned.
This is followed by a delineation of bandhas or mudrās. They are: mūlabandha, oḍḍiyāṇa, jālandhara, khecarī, vajrolī and mahāmudrā.
A long passage in prose, giving a description of ब्रह्मन् the Absolute and the process of च्रेअतिओन् is given as the next subject. प्रणव or Oṁ is its symbol.
The three parts of प्रणव, viz., a, u, and m, and what they signify is expounded next.
Then follows praṇavajapa or repetition of Oṁ with meditation on the light of the आत्मन्.
The other topics discussed towards the end are: certain aspects of प्राणायाम, results of a few yogic practices and a special मुद्रा or posture called ṣaṇmukhī-मुद्रा.

Yogadarśana
------------------------------------------
Introduction
Indian philosophical systems are known as ‘darśanas.’ Unlike the Western philosophical systems, they do not depend solely on लोगिच् and reasoning, but on ‘darśana’ or ‘seeing’ or ‘experiencing’ the truth, in mystical states. Hence the appropriateness of the term. The darśanas have been classified into two groups: the आस्तिक and the नास्तिक. Those that are based on the authority of the वेदस् are called ‘āstika’ and the rest are ‘nāstika.’ The Cārvāka (Materialism), the Jaina and the Bauddha systems come under the latter category and, the षड्-दर्शनस् or the six traditional systems of Hindu philosophy, under the former.
The six traditional systems are: न्याय, Vaiśeṣika, Sāṅkhya, योग, Mīmāṁsā and Vedānta. They generally deal with four topics: existence and nature of ब्रह्मन् or ईश्वर or God; nature of the जीव or the individual सोउल्; च्रेअतिओन् of jagat or the world; मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् as also the disciplines that lead to it.
Sāṅkhya and योग Darśanas
The word ‘Sāṅkhya’ has been derived from ‘saṅkhyā,’ which means ज्ञान or knowledge. Since the Sāṅkhya system of the sage कपिल declares ज्ञान as the sole or primary means of attaining mokṣa—called ‘kaivalya’ in this system—it has been designated as ‘Sāṅkhya-दर्शन’. ‘Saṅkhyā’ also means ‘number’. Since this system has fixed the number of the basic cosmic principles as 24 + 1, it might have earned this appellation for itself.
The Sāṅkhya system accepts only पुरुष (the individual सोउल्) and प्रधान or प्रकृति (nature) as the fundamental realities and does not accept ईश्वर or God. Hence it is sometimes called ‘Nirīśvara-Sāṅkhya’ (‘Sāṅkhya without ईश्वर’). The योगदर्शन which accepts all the principles of the Sāṅkhya and also ईश्वर or God, in addition, has been designated as ‘Seśvara-Sāṅkhya’ (‘Sāṅkhya with ईश्वर’).
In the Sāṅkhya system, tattvajñāna or enquiry into the nature of truth is of primary importance. But the योग system deals primarily with sādhanas or spiritual disciplines. That is why the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि, the basic text of the योग system, begins with the words atha yogānuśāsanam (‘Now, the teaching of योग [is begun].’), instead of the words, ‘jijñāsā’ or ‘mīmāṁsā’ (‘enquiry’).
What is योग?
The word ‘yoga’ can be derived from two verbal roots: yuj (to yoke) or yuj (to concentrate). Hence ‘yoga’ is that which helps a जीव or the individual सोउल् to attain concentration on ईश्वर and ultimate union with him.
The word ‘yoga’ in its several senses has been used in the Ṛgveda (5.81.1) and some of the उपनिषद्स् like the Kaṭha (6.10, 11; 2.12) and the Śvetāśvatara (1.3). The Bhagavadgītā (6.11, 13, 20 and 35) contains many ideas which appear to reflect the teachings of the Yogasūtras (c.f. 2.46; 1.2; 1.12). It is likely that there might have been a more ancient work on योग attributed to हिरण्यगर्भ, and this could have influenced other works.
The Author and His Times
Hindu tradition attributes the origin of the science of योग to हिरण्यगर्भ, an aspect of God himself. Two sages—Sanatkumāra and Jaigiṣavya—are sometimes stated to be the authors of योग-śāstra. However, their works have not been traced till now.
Among the works on योग available now, the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि seems to be the most ancient one. Whether the पतञ्जलि who wrote the bhāṣya or commentary on the sūtras of पाणिनि and the पतञ्जलि of the Yogasūtras are the same or not, has not been conclusively established. A work on आयुर्वेद, also attributed to him, has not been traced so far.
Scholars opine that पतञ्जलि might have lived during the period 200 B. C.—A.

.
The Work
Like the other works of the six darśanas, पतञ्जलि’s treatise also is in the form of sūtras. A sūtra is a brief mnemonic statement with a minimum of letters, but expressing a vast amount knowledge.
The Yogasūtras comprises 195 sūtras spread over four pādas or chapters. They are: Samādhipāda (sūs. 51); Sādhanapāda (sūs. 55); Vibhūtipāda (sūs. 55) and Kaivalyapāda (sūs. 34).
A Sūtra work, by its very nature, is ambiguous, if not obscure, and hence needs a commentary to unravel it. Fortunately for us, the work Yogasūtras has attracted the attention of a number of savants who have enriched the योग literature by their earned commentaries and sub-commentaries.
The Bhāṣya of व्यास is regarded as the basic commentary honoured by almost all the later writers. This व्यास, considered to be different from the traditional वेदव्यास, lived perhaps during the period A.

.
The following are the glosses on this Vyāsabhāṣya:
Tattvavaiśāradī of वाचस्पति मिश्र (A.

-820). Whether the work is really that of the famous teacher of Advaita Vedānta or not, scholars do not seem to agree. The style of writing and the presentation, as also the belief that शङ्कर was a great योगि, lends some support to the view that he is the author of this work.
There are at least six commentaries written directly on the Yogasūtras. They are:
Rājamārttāṇḍavṛtti of Bhojadeva (11th cent.); Yogasūtrapradīpikā of Bhāvāgaṇeśa; Yogasūtravṛtti of Nagojibhaṭṭa; Yogamaṇiprabhā of रामानन्द यति; Yogasiddhāntacandrikā of नारायण Tīrtha and Yogasudhākara of सदाशिव Brahmendra (18th cent.).
Philosophy of the Yogasūtras
Though the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि is primarily a work heavily oriented towards sādhana or spiritual practice, a basic knowledge of its Sāṅkhyan background is necessary to understand it.
Yogadarśana accepts three funda-mental realities: ईश्वर, puruṣas and प्रधान or प्रकृति.
Puruṣas are the individual souls. They are cidrūpa or of the nature of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and are infinite in number.
The existence of ईश्वर, called ‘Puruṣaviśeṣa’ (‘special or unique पुरुष’) can be known only through the scriptures. He is sarvajña or omniscient. Being untouched by the shackles of प्रकृति he is ever free. He is the ādiguru, the primeval teacher. He is designated by प्रणव or Oṁ. It is by his will and in accordance with the karmas of the puruṣas that प्रकृति, comprising the three guṇas सत्त्व, रजस् and तमस्, evolves into this universe. The evolutes of प्रकृति are महत् (cosmic intellect), अहङ्कार (the ego-principle), मनस् (cosmic मिन्द्), the तन्मात्रस् (subtle elements) and so on, just as in the Sāṅkhyan system.
The पुरुष or the individual सोउल्, somehow—due to अविद्या or nescience—forgets his real nature as pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, gets involved with the evolutes of प्रकृति and suffers all the pangs of birth, death and transmigration. However, when he performs sādhanas—the aṣṭāṅgas or the eight steps of yoga—he once again realises his essential nature and is instantly freed from सṁसार, the cycle of transmigration. Being established in oneself, thus transcending सṁसार, is called ‘kaivalya’.
Yoga as ‘Cittavṛttinirodha’
Patañjali defines योग as cittavṛtti-nirodhaḥ (1.2). When all the vṛttis or modifications of the चित्त or the मिन्द् are controlled and suppressed (= niruddha), the true nature of the पुरुष or the Self is revealed. चित्त is the मिन्द्-stuff that is variously called as अन्तःकरण (the inner instrument), मनस् (the मिन्द्) or बुद्धि (the intellect). The waves of thoughts, feelings and emotions that arise in it due to the impact of the sense-objects upon it through the sense-organs like the eyes and the ears, are called ‘cittavṛttis.’ Though these cittavṛttis appear to be innumerable, they can be classified under five groups: pramāṇa (means of right knowledge), विपर्यय (false-knowledge), विकल्प (mental picture based on hearing a word), निद्रा (sleep) and स्मृति (memory).
Pramāṇa is the means of right knowledge. The प्रमाणस् are three: प्रत्यक्ष (direct perception), अनुमान (inference) and āgama (words of reliable persons and the scriptures).
Viparyaya is false knowledge as that of seeing a snake in a rope in semi-darkness.
Vikalpa is the mental picture that arises on hearing a word or words like “Rāhu’s head” (Rāhu, the malefic planet has only the head and no other part of the body).
Nidrā or sleep is that condition of मिन्द् where its modifications arise out of a preponderance of तमस्.
Smṛti is the memory of previous experiences.
These cittavṛttis when they produce क्लेश or suffering to the पुरुष due to अविद्या (ignorance), अस्मिता (egoism) and so on, are called kliṣṭa. When they help the पुरुष to free himself from them, they become ‘akliṣṭa’.
The चित्त or the मिन्द् has five states: क्षिप्त (impulsive), mūḍha (dull), vikṣipta (distracted), ekāgra (one-pointed) and niruddha (inhibited). योग is not possible in the first three states since the मिन्द् is in the grip of रजस् and तमस्. When सत्त्व predominates, the मिन्द् can attain one-pointedness leading it to सम्प्रज्ञात-समाधि (state of perfect concentration where there is a clear चोग्नितिओन् of the object). In the last, the niruddha state, there is a total suppression of all modifica-tions, leading to असम्प्रज्ञात-समाधि, where no object is cognized and the पुरुष remains established in his intrinsic state. Then he becomes a mukta, a liberated सोउल्, freed from all the trammels of प्रकृति.
Obstacles to Yoga
Patañjali calls the obstacles to योग as ‘antarāyas’ (‘that which comes in between’) and lists them as nine (1.30): व्याधि (illness), स्त्यान (apathy), सṁशय (doubt), प्रमाद (heedlessness), आलस्य (laziness), अविरति (lack of renunciation), भ्रान्तिदर्शन (misconception), अलब्ध-भूमिकत्व (failure to attain yogic states) and अनवस्थितत्व (instability in the state).
Illness has to be remedied by medical treatment. Apathy has to be overcome by exercising will-power. Doubt must be countered by faith in the scriptures and the preceptor. Heedlessness must be abolished by eternal vigilance. Laziness should be conquered by healthy activity. Lack of renunciation should be nullified through विवेक (discrimination) and वैराग्य (detachment). The last three obstacles must be tackled as per the advice of a competent preceptor.
Patañjali names five more obstacles to योग (1.31) since they too distract the मिन्द्. They are: दुःख (pain), दौर्मनस्य (frustration), अङ्गमेजयत्व (restlessness of the limbs of the body), श्वास and प्रश्वास (spasmodic breathing in or out). They too have to be countered by appropriate remedies.
Some Practical Hints
Patañjali gives quite a few suggestions which help an aspirant to ward off the obstacles to योग and attain greater concentration, ultimately leading to समाधि or mystical experience of the self. Out of these, वैराग्य (detachment or the spirit of renunciation) and अभ्यास (constant practice) come first (1.12). The former helps one to take the मिन्द् away from the sense-objects whereas the latter leads it towards the Self or God.
Other hints given are: an attitude of friendship (maitrī) towards those who are happy (instead of feeling jealous of them); compassion (karuṇā) towards those who are suffering; controlling the prāṇic energy by regulating the breath; meditating on the light in the centre of one’s heart; contemplating on the minds of great persons; repeatedly remembering highly elevating द्रेअम्स् if one had had them; and contemplating on the forms of gods and goddesses or प्लनेत्स् like the मोओन् or the psychic centres in one’s own body.
All these methods help the spiritual aspirant to gain peace of मिन्द् as also greater control over it.
Aṣṭāṅgas or Eight Steps
The पुरुष or the jīvātman (indi-vidual सोउल्) is in bondage because of his inordinate attachment to his body-मिन्द् complex, which is a product of प्रकृति. The aim of योग is ‘viyoga’ (separating) of the पुरुष from the clutches of प्रकृति. This comes about by विवेकख्याति or the knowledge that प्रकृति and पुरुष are essentially separate from each other (khyāti = knowledge; विवेक = discrimi-nation).
The Yogasūtras prescribes a graded discipline comprising eight steps, called the ‘aṣṭāṅgas’ of योग. They are: यम (restraint), नियम (observances), आसन (posture), प्राणायाम (control of vital currents), प्रत्याहार (state of withdrawal), धारणा (concentration), ध्यान (meditation) and समाधि (total absorption). Out of these, the first five are considered as ‘bahiraṅgas’ (external aids) and the last three as ‘antaraṅgas’ (internal aids) to योग.
Ahiṁsā (non-injury), सत्य (truth), अस्तेय (non-stealing), ब्रह्मचर्य (continence) and अपरिग्रह (non-acceptance of gifts) constitute यम, the first step.
Niyama includes शौच (cleanliness), सन्तोष (contentment), तपस् (austerity of body, speech and मिन्द्), स्वाध्याय (study of holy books and repetition of mantras like Oṁ), and ईश्वरप्रणिधान (devotion to God).
The former contribute to social harmony and the latter to personal purity. The three disciplines of तपस्, स्वाध्याय and ईश्वरप्रणिधान are grouped together by पतञ्जलि and christened as ‘Kriyāyoga’. It is effective as a shortcut to योग.
Āsana is that posture in which one can sit steadily and comfortably for the practice of योग. प्राणायाम is controlling the vital airs in the body, through the regulation of breathing. When the sense-organs are withdrawn from the sense-objects they remain merged as it were, in the मिन्द्. This is called प्रत्याहार.
The next three disciplines—dhāraṇā, ध्यान and samādhi—are actually three continuous steps of the same process. In धारणा, the मिन्द् is fixed on the object of concentration. When this concentration becomes uninterrupted, like the oil being poured from one vessel into another, it is ध्यान. When ध्यान ripens into a state of total absorption on the object, so much so, that the aspirant is not aware of even his own existence, it is called समाधि. समाधि can be attained by ईश्वर-praṇidhāna or devotion to God also (1.23).
Patañjali terms these three steps together as ‘saṁyama’. And, this सṁयम should always be on one and the same object.
Yogasiddhis
The belief that one can attain supernatural powers by तपस् and by the grace of God is very ancient. पतञ्जलि describes quite a few of such powers in the second and the third chapters in order to generate faith in the minds of the ordinary seekers of truth. For instance, he declares that while in the company of a person who is well-established in the virtue of अहिṁसा, even animals inimical to one another (like a tiger and a cow) will live in peace and mutual harmony. The words of a person rooted in सत्य will be infallible. One who observes अपरिग्रह very strictly can get a knowledge of his past and future lives (vide 2.35, 36 and 39).
Saṁyama on different objects will endow the योगि with several occult powers. For instance, by सṁयम on the five elements like पृथ्वी (earth) and ap (water), the योगि can get अष्टसिद्धिस् or the eight-fold powers like अणिमा (power to become atomic in size), mahimā (power to grow to any large size) and so on (3.44, 45). Some of the other powers given in the work are: thought-reading, disappearance from view, getting enormous strength, understanding the language of animals and other creatures, and so on.
However, पतञ्जलि, who as a scientist of मिन्द्, describes these powers (since they are part of the science), also cautions the aspirant of योग not to seek them. The temptation for these powers can lead him away from the goal of his life, viz., कैवल्य or लिबेरतिओन्. But, after the attainment of kaivalya—since he may continue to live for some more time due to prārabdha-कर्म (the कर्म that has started this life)—he will have those powers and can safely use them for the good of mankind.
Conclusion
The योगदर्शन is not only ancient but also very practical. Even the Vedāntic systems accept its sādhana aspects. Modern psychologists too are discovering its utility in guarding or in regaining mental health. Methods and techniques of योग are becoming quite popular all over the world. The first two steps—yama and niyama—can contribute to the well-being of the individual as well as of the society. The various āsanas—better known as yogāsanas—can help in regaining or maintaining one’s health. Thus the योग system is gradually gaining universal acceptance.

Yogatattvopaniṣad
------------------------------------------
The उपनिषद्स् are normally divided into two groups: the major and the minor. Out of the 120 or 125 उपनिषद्स् available in print, the well-known ten उपनिषद्स् (from the Īśāvasyopaniṣad up to the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad) are considered the major ones and the rest as minor. Among the latter, 20 उपनिषद्स् are classed as the योग उपनिषद्स् since their subject matter is mainly centred round योग (Rājayoga and हठयोग).
The Yogatattvopaniṣad belongs to this group. It is assigned to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda and has 142 verses without any internal divisions as chapters.
The following is a brief synoptic summary of its contents:
Some general principles of Advaita Vedānta; the four yogas viz., राजयोग, मन्त्रयोग, हठयोग and लययोग; the eight steps of योग; detailed treatment of प्राणायाम (See PRĀṆĀYĀMA.) and a few bandhas (See MUDRĀ.); meditation on Saguṇa and Nirguṇa aspects of ब्रह्मन्; some mudrās like khecarī; meditation on the प्रणव in the lotus of the heart.

yogāsanas
(‘postures [recommended by the science of] योग’)
------------------------------------------
Yogāsanas are now extremely popular all over the world, mostly as physical exercises. However they are much more than that. Coupled with प्राणायाम (yogic technique of controlling the प्राण or the basic life-force, through special breathing exercises) they act at three levels: the physical body, the vital body and the मिन्द्. When perfected they help the physical body to have strength and stamina, regulate the internal body-chemistry and assist in gaining control over the मिन्द्.
Āsana means a posture (of sitting or standing). According to one view, by imitating the posture of an animal, one can get that animal’s agility or any other special capacity. That is why quite a few योगासनस् are named after some animal or the other (as in Kukkuṭāsana or Mayūrāsana; kukkuṭa = cock; mayūra = peacock).
Though such योगासनस् can be innumerable, thirty-two have been mentioned as more important by the Gheraṇḍa Saṁhitā (Chapter 2), a standard work of हठयोग, more directly concerned with the योगासनस् and प्राणायाम.
Yogāsanas have certain advantages over the gymnastic exercises. They can be practised by all, irrespective of age or sex or health conditions if specific instructions are followed. No external appliance like dumb-bells or barbells or any other device is needed. The yogic exercises reduce the toxins in the body instead of increasing them as done by the other system.
Those who wish to practise योगासनस् are required to observe some general rules. They are:
Organs of evacuation should be empty before practising the योगासनस्.
It is better to do the योगासनस् after bath. Otherwise, there must be a gap of at least 30 minutes for bath after doing them.
Early morning is the best time for doing the योगासनस्.
drinking a glass of warm water before beginning will help.
The place must be clean and airy. A blanket should be spread and the योगासनस् practised on it.
Breathing must be done through the nostrils only.
At the end, sweat should be dried by spreading it with the bare hands and not with a cloth.
Those suffering from some diseases like hypertension should not practise topsy-turvy postures.
Women are advised to avoid some योगासनस् during certain periods or conditions.
Before beginning the regular practice of the योगासनस्, a few preparatory exercises have to be done to loosen the joints and attain flexibility. These include bending, rotating the arms, clenching the hands and movements of the neck. Some exercises for the eyes also are prescribed.
According to the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) आसन is the third of the eight steps of योग. He defines it as that posture in which one can sit comfortably and steadily for a long time, for meditation (vide 2.29, 46, 48). The works on हठयोग recommend the following āsanas for meditation: भद्रासन, पद्मासन, Siddhāsana, Svastikāsana, Vajrāsana and वीरासन.
Out of the several योगासनस् currently in use, the following sixteen are very common:
Ardhamatsyendrāsana
Baddhapadmāsana
Bhujaṅgāsana
Dhanurāsana
Halāsana
Matsyāsana
Mayūrāsana
Merudaṇḍāsana
Paścimottānāsana
Śalabhāsana
Sarvāṅgāsana
Śavāsana
Siṁhāsana
Śīrṣāsana
Utthitadvipādāsana
Utthitatrikoṇāsana
It is best to learn these योगासनस् directly from a competent teacher. Though pictures and descriptions of them are often given in standard works, there is always a chance of going wrong or even getting into trouble.
When practised properly these योगासनस् have either cured or decreased the effects of many ailments. In fact, quite a few have been designed as cures for specific diseases.

Yogaśayanamūrti
------------------------------------------
This is one of the aspects of विष्णु shown as recumbent on शेष or आदिशेष as the couch. He is pale blue or blue with an yellowish tinge. He has two arms. He is blissfully absorbed in योगनिद्रा or yogic slumber.
He may be shown as surrounded by the sages भृगु and मार्कण्डेय as also the āyudhas or weapons like शङ्ख (conch), चक्र (discus), गदा (mace) as personified deities. The two demons, मधु and कैटभ, too are present.

yogavidhi
(‘method of योग’)
------------------------------------------
This is a word that has been used only in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad (6.18).
This Upaniṣad declares at the very end that नचिकेतस् attained ब्रह्मन् after knowing from यम, the god of death, the विद्या (spiritual wisdom) and the योगविधि (the method of योग) in its complete form.
What is this योगविधि? It is a discipline described earlier in the verse 6.10. It consists of withdrawing the five organs of knowledge from their external objects along with the मिन्द्, and make the intellect steady (in ब्रह्मन्).
However, it is not only नचिकेतस् but anyone else too, who follows this योगविधि, that attains the deathless state.

Yogaśikhopaniṣad
------------------------------------------
Though classed among the minor उपनिषद्स् of the योग group, this is a fairly long and exhaustive Upaniṣad. It belongs to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. It is in the form of a dialogue between हिरण्यगर्भ (the disciple) and शिव (the teacher).
There are 390 verses in all, in the anuṣṭubh metre spread over six adhyāyas or chapters.
The first adhyāya (178 verses) deals with a large number of topics. After describing some preliminaries common to Vedāntic scriptures, it deals exhaustively with quite a few topics of हठयोग. The following is a brief list of such topics: purification and refinement of the मिन्द् through योग; necessity of approaching a गुरु or spiritual teacher who is an adept in प्राणायाम; arousing the कुण्डलिनी power (See CAKRAS and TANTRAS.); various kinds of prāṇāyāmas and bandhas (See MUDRĀS and PRĀṆĀYĀMAS.); some yogas like मन्त्रयोग and लययोग; importance of अभ्यास or continuous practice; जीवन्मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन् even while living.
The second adhyāya (22 verses) deals mainly with प्रणव (Oṅkāra) as the mūlamantra (fundamental esoteric formula). It is interesting to note that devotion to the गुरु and God are stressed as all-important in attaining the know-ledge of the Supreme.
The third adhyāya (25 verses) describes Nādabrahman or ब्रह्मन् as sound and its four forms viz., parā, paśyanti, madhyamā and वैखरी (See PARĀ for details.).
The fourth adhyāya (24 verses) puts forward the usual theories of Advaita Vedānta such as the non-existence of the जीव (individual सोउल्) as an independent reality, the world as unreal as the objects seen in a dream and the body as a superimposition on the सोउल् due to अज्ञान or nescience.
The fifth adhyāya (62 verses) describes the body as the residence of विष्णु, the all-pervading Supreme Lord. Then follows an account of the six चक्रस् like मूलाधार. Other topics portrayed are: rousing of the कुण्डलिनी power, खेचरीमुद्रा (See KHECARĪMUDRĀ.), meditation on नारायण in the sahasrāracakra, method of worshipping one’s गुरु and indifference towards सिद्धिस् or yogic powers.
The sixth, the last, adhyāya (79 verses) deals with a few more topics of हठयोग and ज्ञानयोग. They are: method of meditation on the कुण्डलिनी power; description of the suṣumnānāḍī; meditations on the forms of ब्रह्मा in the six चक्रस्; bondage and लिबेरतिओन् depending on the मिन्द् being active or still.
The Upaniṣad ends with the warning that ज्ञान (spiritual wisdom as direct experience) can arise only by practice done according to the instructions of a qualified गुरु.

Yogeśvarī
(‘queen of yogas’)
------------------------------------------
Yogeśvarī is an aspect of the Divine मोथेर्. She is called so, since she provides the benefits of योग to the aspirants who are practising it sincerely (vide देवी-purāṇa, Chapter 45). योग is defined as the integrated approach of the मिन्द् and the senses towards itself, by the आत्मन् or the Self.
She is also called आदिशक्ति (the Primeval Power) who emerged out of the mouth (as light) of शिव during his encounter with the demon Andhaka.
Sometimes she is counted as the eighth mātṛkā, after the seven (Sapta-mātṛkās).
She is identified with रक्तचामुण्डा also. Iconographical works describe her as dark in colour with three eyes and a long tongue. She has ten hands and rides on a crow.
She is worshipped in the Maha-rashtra region as Ambeyogai or Jogeśvarī.

Yogamāyā
------------------------------------------
The power of ईश्वर or God, by which he creates, sustains and withdraws the world, is called Māyā or योगमाया. She is pictured as a goddess and considered an aspect of दुर्गा.
According to the Bhāgavata (10.3.47) she was born to यशोदा on the same day as कृष्ण was born to देवकी. She was exchanged with कृष्ण, by Vasudeva.
When कṁस, the demon-king of मथुरा, tried to kill her she escaped from his grip, assumed her real form as दुर्गा and warned him.
Her birthday is celebrated in some places on the day next to कृष्ण’s.
The Bhagavadgītā (7.25) refers to her as the power of delusion.

yoginīs
(‘women with yogic powers,’ ‘goddesses’)
------------------------------------------
In the tāntrik practices, the male sādhaka, called a योगि, needs the help of a mate in certain occult rites. Such women, ceremonially infilled with great powers, are designated as योगिनीस्.
The word is also used to indicate the goddesses emanating out of the effulgence of आदिशक्ति or the Primeval Goddess. Their number may be 8 or 62 or 64. Their names have been mentioned in some of the पुराणस् and other works like the Bṛhan-nandikeśvarapurāṇa, Skandapurāṇa and the Mantramahodadhi.
A few of these names may be mentioned here: नारायणी, शाकम्भरी, Bhīmā, Caṇḍaghaṇṭā, Bhadrakālī, कृष्ण-पिङ्गला, Jalodarī, शाकिनी, Kuleśī, Nakulī, डाकिनी and Hākinī.
During worship, sometimes, a group of eight योगिनीस् is selected. They are: Maṅgalā, पिङ्गला, Dhanyā, Bhrāmarī, Bhadrikā, Ulkā, Siddhā, Saṅkaṭā.
According to another view, the योगिनीस् are divinities associated with the eight vargas or groups of letters of the alphabets such as a-varga, ka-varga and ca-varga.

Yogasārasaṅgraha
(‘abridged edition of the essence of योगदर्शन’)
------------------------------------------
The basic text of the योगदर्शन or the Philosophy of योग is the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.). This work has several commentaries, of which the Vyāsabhāṣya is considered the primary authority. विज्ञानभिक्षु (16th century A. D.) who has written a scholarly gloss on it, called the Yogavārttika, has beautifully summarised the entire work in this treatise, the Yogasārasaṅgraha. It is in simple prose, often interspersed with plenty of relevant quotations culled from various authoritative texts.
There are four chapters called aṁśas.
A brief synopsis of the contents may now be attempted.

First Chapter (Yogasvarūpa or Nature of योग and its Utility)
Five functions of the चित्त or the मिन्द्; nirodha defined as withdrawal of the function of the मिन्द्; results of two kinds of samādhis (perfect meditation), viz., cessation of pain and attainment of मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्; four kinds of समाधि, which are part of samprajñātasamādhi (conscious or concrete समाधि); two kinds of asamprajñātasamādhi (abstract समाधि).

Second Chapter (Yogasādhana or Yogic Practices)
Abhyāsa (repeated efforts) and वैराग्य (detachment) as primary means to योग; parikarmas or special practices that help in controlling the मिन्द्; on क्रियायोग comprising तपस् (austerity), स्वाध्याय (study of the scriptures) and ईश्वरप्रणिधान (devotion to God); five kleśas or troubles of the मिन्द् and their elimination; the eight steps of meditation like यम, नियम and so on; importance of the last three steps.

Third Chapter (Yogasiddhis or Powers)
Dhāraṇā (fixing the मिन्द् on the object of concentration), ध्यान (continuous concentration) and समाधि (perfect meditation) defined as सṁयम; various kinds of सिद्धिस् or powers arising out of सṁयम on various objects.

Fourth Chapter (Kaivalya or लिबेरतिओन्)
Kaivalya (isolation or लिबेरतिओन्) defined; reconciling the view of योग system on लिबेरतिओन् with the views of other schools; कैवल्य is cessation of all दुःख or sorrow; points of difference between योग and Sāṅkhya philosophies; two new points—the Sphoṭa and Manovaibhava (powers of the अन्तःकरण or the internal organ). (See SPHOṬAVĀDA.)
This treatise has been considered one of the best books on the योग philosophy of पतञ्जलि because of its clarity as also comprehensive nature.
See also VIJÑĀNABHIKṢU.

Yoga
------------------------------------------
This word is used in several senses. When derived from the root ‘yuj samādhau’ it means perfect concentration of मिन्द्. If derived from another root, ‘yujir yoge’, it means ‘to unite’. Combining these two senses one can say that it stands for that art and science of concentration of मिन्द् which helps the spiritual aspirant to ultimately unite his individual सोउल् (jīvātman) with the Supreme सोउल् (Paramātman).
The योगदर्शन of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) fits in with this description. See YOGADARŚANA for details.
However, in general, this word is often loosely used for any spiritual discipline. A few of them are listed below, arranged in the alphabetical order:
Abhāvayoga
The Taittirīya Upaniṣad (2.1) describes the evolution of the world from the आत्मन् (same as ब्रह्मन्), through the five elements like the आकाश (space, ether) right up to पुरुष (human being). In Abhāvayoga, the aspirant has to meditate on the reverse process, merging each succeeding product in the preceding one, finally arriving at the आत्मन्-principle which is nirguṇa (without attributes) and nirākāra (without forms) and is pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. In this state of योग, the whole world appearance has disappeared (abhāva = nothingness) and only the आत्मन् is experienced.
Amanaskayoga
This is the योग in which the मिन्द् is prevented from rising in the form of vṛttis (waves) and made absolutely still, whereby the आत्मन् is experienced. Certain disciplines of हठयोग like the खेचरीमुद्रा (See KHECARĪMUDRĀ.) have to be practised first.
Aṣṭāṅgayoga
The योगदर्शन of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) is named Aṣṭāṅgayoga since it consists of eight limbs (aṣṭa = eight; अङ्ग = limb or steps). See YOGADARŚANA for details.
Bhaktiyoga
See BHAKTI and BHAKTIYOGA.
Bhāvayoga
After practising mantrajapa (repetition of the divine name) coupled with प्राणायाम (control of breath) for quite some time, if the जप is given up, leading to the direct experience of the divine presence, it is भावयोग.
Buddhiyoga
See BUDDHIYOGA.
Dhyānayoga
See DHYĀNAYOGA.
Haṭhayoga
See HAṬHAYOGA.
Jñānayoga
See JÑĀNAYOGA.
Karmayoga
See KARMAYOGA.
Kriyāyoga
See KRIYĀYOGA.
Kuṇḍalinīyoga
The योग by which the कुण्डलिनी power is taken up through the six चक्रस् right up to the seventh, is called Kuṇḍalinīyoga.
See CAKRAS and KUṆḌALINĪ.
Layayoga
This is another name for कुण्डलिनी-योग.
Mahāyoga
This is the stage next to Abhāvayoga wherein the aspirant will experience his oneness with शिव or God.
Mantrayoga
See MANTRAYOGA.
Nādayoga
Brahman is all-pervading pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. When he wills to create the world (vide Chāndogya Upaniṣad

and 3; Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6; Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.1) a स्पन्द or नाद (vibration or sound) appears in him. This will gradually evolve into this multiplicity of the universe. That नाद is represented by प्रणव or Oṁ. meditation on this नाद ultimately leading to the dissolution of the मिन्द् and arising of supreme know-ledge is called Nādayoga.
Rājayoga
This is the same as the योग taught by पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.). See YOGADARŚANA for details.
Śivayoga
Achieving the unity of the jīvātman (the individual सोउल्) with परमात्मन् is Śivayoga according to the scriptures of शैविस्म्. It has five steps: arcana (worship of the chosen deity); anusandhāna (meditating on the form of the deity); भक्ति (cultivation of devotion); विद्या (receiving the मन्त्र); vrata (strictly following the disciplines imposed by the गुरु and the scriptures).
Sparśayoga
When मन्त्रयोग is practised along with प्राणायाम, it is called स्पर्शयोग.
Tantrayoga
The path of spiritual discipline described in the works on तन्त्रस् consisting of षट्चक्रभेद (piercing the six चक्रस्) is called Tantrayoga.
(See CAKRAS for details.)
Tārakayoga
Just as one burning lamp can light another, a perfect गुरु (spiritual master) can pass on his spiritual power to a qualified or worthy disciple even by a touch. This is called Tārakayoga. It is also called śaktipāta or bequeathing spiritual power.
In Hindu अस्त्रोलोग्य्, the word योग is used in a technical sense to indicate the fourth limb of the पञ्चाङ्ग or almanac. (See PAÑCĀṄGA.)

Yogavārttika
------------------------------------------
On the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) there is an ancient and original commentary known as the Vyāsabhāṣya by व्यास. On this, there are two well-known glosses: the Tattvavaiśāradī of वाचस्पति मिश्र (A.
) and the Yoga-vārttika of विज्ञानभिक्षु (A.

).
The Yogavārttika is a lucid explanation of the Vyāsabhāṣya. However it often differs from the views given in the Tattvavaiśāradī.
Vijñānabhikṣu seems more inclined towards bringing the साङ्ख्य-योग philosophy nearer to the traditional Vedānta.
See also VIJÑĀNABHIKṢU.

Yogavāsiṣṭha
------------------------------------------
This is an extremely popular work, especially among the followers of Advaita Vedānta. It is an extensive philosophical poem spread over six prakaraṇas or chapters containing nearly 32,000 verses, (according to tradition) though the printed versions contain much less (23,734 verses). It might have been composed during the 8th century A. D. It is by an unknown author while tradition assigns it to the sage वाल्मीकि.
It is known by several other names such as Yogavāsiṣṭharāmāyaṇa, Mahā-rāmāyaṇa and Jñānavāsiṣṭha also.
It seems to have influenced several later works like Annapūrṇa Upaniṣad, Mahopaniṣad, the Mānasollāsa of सुरेश्वर (A.
) on the Dakṣiṇāmūrti-stotra of शङ्कर (A.

-820) and the Jīvanmuktiviveka of विद्यारण्य (14th century A. D.).
It has several commentaries. Some of them are: Vāsiṣṭharāmāyaṇacandrikā by Advayāraṇya; Tātparyaprakāśa of Ānandabodhendrasarasvatī; Padacandrikā by Mādhavasarasvatī.
A few summaries of the work are also available such as Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha of Gauḍa Abhinanda (9th century A. D.) and Vāsiṣṭhasāragūḍhārtha by Rāmā-nandatīrtha. These works again have their own commentaries written by scholars.
The treatise begins in a dramatic manner containing stories within stories, and ends with a long dialogue between the sage वसिष्ठ and राम, the son of king दशरथ of अयोध्या.
The first section called Vairāgya-prakaraṇa describes the वैराग्य or intense dispassion of राम due to disillusionment with the transitory nature of the world. At the request of the king दशरथ, the sage वसिष्ठ tries to enlighten him. This is the setting of the entire work.
Mumukṣuvyavahāraprakaraṇa, the second section, tells राम that disillusionment with the world, because it is evanescent, should lead to the dawn of wisdom. The conviction that one is in bondage because one feels that the world is real and of one’s own ego as real should lead to the cultivation of the four qualities of शम (tranquillity), vicāra (rational investigation), सन्तोष (contentment) and sādhusaṅgama (the company of the wise). Here, the sage वसिष्ठ stresses the importance of pauruṣa (self-effort) and that it can help overcome even the effect of past karmas.
The next section called Utpatti-prakaraṇa deals with सृष्टि or च्रेअतिओन्. वसिष्ठ is a thoroughgoing idealist. According to him this world is a manifestation of the mind—the मिन्द् of ब्रह्मा (the creator) by his सङ्कल्प or will. Even as the ocean alone is real and not the waves, though they appear and disappear, it is ब्रह्मन् the ultimate Reality that is real and not the world.
An analysis of the three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् is resorted to, to prove this point.
Since the world arises by the सङ्कल्प (thought, desire) of ब्रह्मन्, it is experienced by all of us as the same, tinted, however, with our own सङ्कल्प.
The fourth section is called Sthiti-prakaraṇa. The world continues to exist only so long as the सङ्कल्प or desire is there. The world-experience is maintained as long as the मिन्द् is active and outward-looking. This is proved by taking the example of avasthātraya or the three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. It is vāsanās (inclinations and predispositions of the मिन्द्) that are responsible for the continuance of world-experience.
The fifth section is termed the Upāsanāprakaraṇa, teaching the art of calming the मिन्द्. This calming of the मिन्द् is similar to the deep-sleep state. The techniques of destruction of the vāsanās or vāsanākṣaya are described here, leading to manonāśa—the destruction of the tendencies in the मिन्द् to rise in the form of mental waves. ज्ञान or knowledge of the Self is the chief technique.
Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa is the last chapter. This is the longest part and has two sections, the pūrvārdha (earlier part) and the uttarārdha (later part). It has a number of stories and is highly repetitious. निर्वाण or लिबेरतिओन् is the realisation of the identity of the Self with the Absolute or ब्रह्मन्. Since bondage arises by the false identification of the Self with the body, its reversal through a critical inquiry leads to this लिबेरतिओन्. Hence, neither worship nor devotion to God will be of any use in this path!
Liberation is possible for everyone here and now. The liberated man, called jīvanmukta—one who is free even while living—is a normal person who continues to live in the world and fulfil all the duties of his life. He is equanimous under all circumstances of life, never attached to anything.
This treatise lays great stress on pauruṣa or self-effort. The subject of प्राणायाम (control of प्राण or the life-force) is also dealt with in detail. प्राण is essentially of the form of स्पन्द or vibration.
Seven stages of spiritual progress are also described. They are: prathama-bhūmikā (study and association with saintly persons); vicāraṇā (critical thinking); asaṅgabhāvanā (dissociation from all passions); vilāpanī (right understanding that the world-appearance is false); śuddhasaṁvit-मय-ānandarūpa (a state of pure knowledge and bliss); suṣupta-sadṛśasthiti (a state similar to deep sleep, full of bliss); turyātīta (transcendental state got after death).
The fifth is the state of the jīvanmukta.
As regards the sādhanas or spiritual disciplines the Yogavāsiṣṭha advises the aspirant to study sacchāstras or right kind of scriptures and cleanse the मिन्द् by getting rid of राग (attachment), द्वेष (hatred), तमस् (ignorance), krodha (anger), मद (arrogance or pride) and mātsarya (jealousy).
Unlike शङ्कर (A.

-820), वसिष्ठ declares that a joint operation of कर्म (action) and ज्ञान (knowledge) is necessary for reaching the goal.
Great stress is also laid on वासना-kṣaya (destruction of the root-inclinations) and manonāśa (destruction of the tendencies in the मिन्द् that forcibly arise), with the help of tattvajñāna (knowledge of the truth), the three practices always going together.
The work abounds in several interesting stories and analogies.
A few of them may be briefly set out here:
On the advice of his ड़थेर्, the sage व्यास, शुक goes to the king जनक to learn about ब्रह्मन्. Though severely tested, he comes out successful and is taught by him.
There is a long and interesting story of the king पद्म and his queen Līlā in the Utpattiprakaraṇa. The two were very much attached to each other. The queen Līlā prays to the goddess सरस्वती and obtains the boon that when her husband dies, his सोउल् should continue to live within her room. Even though the king पद्म dies, his सोउल् is confined to the room as promised by the goddess. His various experiences are seen mysteriously by the queen Līlā. Ulti-mately the सोउल् of the king re-enters his body. He is revived and lives happily.
In an allegorical story, the human मिन्द् is described as a mad man having a thousand hands and eyes. He constantly beats himself and wanders in a dense forest. This shows the self-torturing nature of the मिन्द्.
A magician hypnotises a king. The king then experiences a long series of events within a short period. This is just to show that all things in this world are relative, including time and space.
Through the story of the sage शुक्राचार्य, it is shown how a जीव transmigrates due to intense desires and attachments.
Dāśūra was a sage who was upset by his ड़थेर्’s death. He then tried to get peace of मिन्द् through austerities and performance of sacrifices but failed. Finally he got it by meditation on the आत्मन् or the Self.
पुण्य and Pāvana were brothers. The former was an enlightened person whereas the latter was not. When their ड़थेर् died Pāvana wept bitterly. पुण्य then revealed to him how he had had innumerable fathers in various births and hence how it was futile to sorrow like that.
The king प्रह्लाद had neglected the duties of the State, by constantly immersing himself in समाधि. Lord विष्णु awakened him and advised him to perform his duties which were equally important.
Gādhi was a ब्राह्मण devotee of god विष्णु. He worshipped विष्णु to know something about his Māyā-power. विष्णु granted the boon. Once, when this devotee, while bathing in a river, dipped his head in water, he had a vision of a wonderful series of events involving himself and taking several years. When he regained his normal state, he discovered through a traveller that all these incidents were true and took place in a distant country.
In the story of Kāka-bhuśuṇḍa, the sage in the form of a crow, वसिष्ठ is taught the science of प्राणायाम by which one can live a very long life.
A vetāla (the malevolent spirit of a dead man) used to put difficult questions to human beings he met and would devour them if they could not answer. He once met an enlightened king who answered all the questions properly. So, he could not harm him at all!
भगीरथ was a king who renounced everything to realise ब्रह्मन्. After realisation he was once requested by the people of another country whose king had died, to be their king. He accepted their offer and ruled wisely. This shows that a man of knowledge can also be a man of action!
The story of the king Śikhidhvaja of Mālva and his queen चूडाला is the longest of all. Hankering after true happiness and peace they start practising spiritual disciplines. चूडाला, through discriminative knowledge, realises the Self first. Her husband Śikhidhvaja does not succeed even after severe austerities. चूडाला, out of her love and compassion for him, succeeds in making him realise the Self by adopting some clever plans. She later tests him in various ways to find out whether his realisation is true and steady. When she finds him truly established in the highest knowledge of the Self, she brings him back to the kingdom to rule over it like a perfectly free and wise man.
There was a very poor woodcutter. He used to go to a forest in search of wood every day and supported his family by selling the wood thus collected. By constantly striving to better his earnings, he one day found the philosopher’s stone. This solved his problem permanently. This story shows how constant efforts at perfection, done according to the instructions of the teacher and the scriptures, will surely succeed one day.
Incidentally, this wonderful work touches upon some other topics also. It is opined that vāsanās are responsible to bring the सोउल् back to other lives. Hence, śrāddhas or obsequial ceremonies to the dead are not of much use.
As regards ritualistic worship, it is ātmapūja or worship of the Self through bodha (understanding), sāmya (sense of equality towards all) and शम (calmness of मिन्द्) that really matters. Other ingredients which are helpful are: मैत्री (friendliness towards all); karuṇā (compassion towards the lowly and the suffering); mudita (delight towards those who are happy) and upekṣā (conscious indifference towards the evildoers).
Mūrtipūjā or image-worship is considered equal to बालक्रीडा or child-play.
On the whole, the Yogavāsiṣṭha is a work that challenges the intellect by its uncompromising लोगिच् and is, at the same time, exhilarating by its beautiful poetry.
